title: Infective Endocarditis: Recognition, Blood Cultures and Urgent Referral

evidenceAudit.scope: Adults with suspected infective endocarditis (IE) in the emergency department (ED) or ward: recognition, modified Duke criteria, blood cultures, echocardiography, endocarditis team, surgical urgency, selected organism-directed treatment and prevention before dental procedures. Uses the 2023 European Society of Cardiology (ESC) guideline (key points and Table 6) and the 2015 American Heart Association (AHA) scientific statement.
findings: Rebuilt from the thin 21 Oct 2026 version: Duke criteria with definite/possible definitions, blood culture standard, imaging sequence, surgery timing, six management steps and a prevention branch with paediatric doses added.

Removed the previous methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) and Enterococcus rows: their cited ESC page numbers (pp. 67–71) do not match the published guideline (pp. 3948–4042) and the ESC regimen tables could not be opened to re-verify them.
Remaining doses trace to AHA 2015 Table 7 and ESC 2023 Table 6, opened on 22 Oct 2026.
unverifiedSections: ESC 2023 Recommendation Tables 7–10 (organism-directed and empirical regimens) and Table 10 (2023 diagnostic criteria) could not be opened; the Duke criteria shown are from AHA 2015. Staphylococcal and enterococcal regimens and empirical therapy are left to the endocarditis team and infectious diseases (AHA 2015 Class I recommendation).
AHA 2015 lists penicillin G first in Table 7 without stated preference; it is marked preferred.
No Saudi national endocarditis guideline was found.
Named examples under vascular and immunological phenomena (Janeway lesions, Osler nodes, Roth spots) follow standard modified Duke wording but were not visible in the opened excerpt.
Pathophysiology statement on bacterial adhesion is clinical description.
CKD and CLD lines come from the platform batch-01 table and were not re-opened in this task.
Typical adult reference ranges are not from the cited sources; local laboratory ranges apply.

pathophysiology.summary: Bacteria in the blood adhere to damaged or prosthetic valves and form vegetations. Vegetations destroy valves, causing heart failure, and fragment, causing emboli; vegetations over 10 mm carry high embolic risk (AHA 2015, p. 1441). Immune complexes cause vascular and immunological phenomena counted in the Duke criteria (AHA 2015, Table 3). Prosthetic-valve endocarditis carries about twice the in-hospital mortality of native-valve disease (ESC 2023, Section Prosthetic valve endocarditis).
keyMechanisms: Prosthetic valves, previous endocarditis and cyanotic congenital heart disease carry the highest risk (ESC 2023 via ACC, point 1).
Vegetations cause valve destruction and heart failure (AHA 2015, Table 5).
Embolism; vegetation over 10 mm is high risk (AHA 2015, p. 1441).
Prosthetic-valve disease has about twice the mortality (ESC 2023, Section Prosthetic valve endocarditis).

symptoms: Focal neurological symptoms from emboli (ESC 2023 via ACC, point 6).
Back or joint pain from musculoskeletal involvement (ESC 2023 via ACC, point 6).
physicalSigns: Vascular phenomena: major arterial emboli, septic pulmonary infarcts, mycotic aneurysm, Janeway lesions (AHA 2015, Table 3).
Immunological phenomena: glomerulonephritis, Osler nodes, Roth spots (AHA 2015, Table 3).
redFlags: Refractory pulmonary oedema or cardiogenic shock — emergency surgery within 24 hours (ESC 2023 via ACC, point 5).
New atrioventricular block suggesting abscess (ESC 2023 via ACC, point 6).
Stroke or transient ischaemic attack (ESC 2023 via ACC, point 7).
Blood cultures still positive after 7 days of appropriate treatment (ESC 2023, Figure 3).
precipitants: Prosthetic valve or ventricular assist device (ESC 2023 via ACC, point 1).
Untreated cyanotic congenital heart disease (ESC 2023 via ACC, point 1).

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Positive cultures with no valve lesion on transthoracic and transoesophageal imaging (ESC 2023 via ACC, point 3).
Negative blood cultures and serology; different clinical criteria.
Mass attached to the atrial septum without positive cultures.

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Typical organisms from 2 separate cultures, persistently positive cultures, or a single culture for Coxiella burnetii or phase 1 IgG titre 1:800 or more (AHA 2015, Table 3).
Oscillating intracardiac mass on a valve or supporting structures (AHA 2015, Table 3); valve or prosthetic involvement on imaging (ESC 2023).
Predisposing heart condition or injection drug use; fever above 38 °C; vascular phenomena; immunological phenomena; microbiological evidence short of a major criterion (AHA 2015, Table 3).
Definite: 2 major, or 1 major plus 3 minor, or 5 minor. Possible: 1 major plus 1 minor, or 3 minor (AHA 2015, Table 2).

ruleIn.expectedFinding: Typical organism in 2 or more separate sets, or persistent bacteraemia
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: From different venepuncture sites, first and last at least 1 hour apart, before antibiotics (Class I).

clinicalManagement.title: Cultures before antibiotics
actions: Take at least 3 blood-culture sets from different sites, first and last at least 1 hour apart (AHA 2015, Recommendation 1).
If unstable, take cultures quickly and do not delay treatment.

clinicalManagement.title: Echocardiography
actions: TTE first; TOE if TTE negative with ongoing suspicion or any prosthetic valve (ESC 2023 via ACC, point 3).
Repeat in 5–7 days if suspicion remains (ESC 2023 via ACC, point 3).

clinicalManagement.title: Endocarditis team
actions: Involve cardiology, imaging, cardiac surgery, infectious diseases and microbiology (ESC 2023 via ACC, point 2).
Infectious diseases consultation defines the empirical regimen (AHA 2015, Class I, p. 1445).
Complicated cases go to a Heart Valve Centre with on-site surgery (ESC 2023 via ACC, point 2).

clinicalManagement.title: Decide surgical urgency
actions: Emergency (within 24 hours): refractory pulmonary oedema or cardiogenic shock (ESC 2023 via ACC, point 5).
Urgent (3–5 days): heart failure, uncontrolled local infection, or vegetation 10 mm or more after an embolic event (ESC 2023 via ACC, point 5).
Significant haemorrhagic stroke: consider delaying surgery at least 4 weeks (ESC 2023 via ACC, point 7).

clinicalManagement.title: Organism-directed treatment
actions: Native valve 2–6 weeks; prosthetic valve at least 6 weeks; first 2 weeks inpatient intravenous (ESC 2023 via ACC, point 4).
No aminoglycosides for staphylococcal native-valve disease; rifampicin only with foreign material; daptomycin, if used, 10 mg/kg once daily (ESC 2023 via ACC, point 4).
Highly penicillin-susceptible streptococci: see Medicines (AHA 2015, Table 7).

clinicalManagement.title: Outpatient phase and follow-up
actions: Outpatient parenteral therapy only if stable after at least 10 days of intravenous treatment (7 days after surgery) (ESC 2023, Recommendation Table 11).
Oral step-down only after TOE shows no local progression (ESC 2023 via ACC, outpatient note).
Repeat blood cultures after finishing antibiotics; dental review and long-term surveillance (ESC 2023 via ACC, point 8).

Penicillin allergy: Sources differ: the BNF advises avoiding it only after anaphylaxis or another immediate reaction to a penicillin (or with any cephalosporin allergy) and otherwise allows use with monitoring; some product information (for example ceftriaxone) lists any penicillin hypersensitivity as a contraindication. Alternative: Vancomycin (the vancomycin row in this branch; AHA 2015 Table 7).

CKD: No dose change if liver function is normal; creatinine clearance below 10 mL/min: maximum 2 g/day — for meningitis doses take pharmacist advice and monitor levels (product information). [batch-01 renal/hepatic table; label not re-opened in this task]

CLD: No dose change if renal function is normal; combined severe renal and hepatic impairment: monitor plasma levels (product information). [batch-01 renal/hepatic table; label not re-opened in this task]
monitoring: Liver tests and full blood count.
contraindications: Cephalosporin allergy, or anaphylaxis to a penicillin.

medicationPlan.note: Empirical treatment and staphylococcal, enterococcal or culture-negative regimens are set by the endocarditis team and infectious diseases. Give one drug per step. ESC 2023 does not recommend clindamycin for prophylaxis. Paediatric, penicillin-allergy, chronic kidney disease (CKD) and chronic liver disease (CLD) lines on every row. SFDA registration not verified.

guidelineComparison.note: Shown as each source states it; not merged.

learningObjectives: Take blood cultures correctly before antibiotics.
keyPoints: Three culture sets before the first dose.
Refractory pulmonary oedema or shock: surgery within 24 hours.
pitfalls: Starting antibiotics for fever before cultures.
Accepting a negative TTE in a prosthetic valve.

patientEducation: Explain the long antibiotic course and why blood tests and scans are repeated.
Report fever, breathlessness or new neurological symptoms after discharge.
Keep good oral hygiene and attend dental reviews (ESC 2023 via ACC, point 8).
lifestyleAndDiet: Offer addiction treatment to people who inject drugs (ESC 2023 via ACC, point 8).
dischargeCriteria: Outpatient therapy only after at least 10 days of intravenous treatment and clinical stability (ESC 2023, Recommendation Table 11).
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Repeat blood cultures after finishing antibiotics; long-term clinical and echocardiographic surveillance; relapse with the same organism needs a search for a persistent focus (ESC 2023 via ACC, point 8).
